common_name: Lagos Spinach (Soko Yokoto, Edible Celosia Greens)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed to at least 65°F, sowing thickly since this leaf-type strain of Celosia argentea is grown for cut-and-come-again greens rather than for its flower plumes.

directions: Lagos spinach is the same species as ornamental cockscomb and plumed celosia, but grown as a leaf vegetable across West Africa, where the mild, slightly peppery young leaves and tender stem tips known as soko yokoto are a staple green in soups and stews. Sow thickly and thin as you harvest, since crowding the plants slightly keeps the leaves tender and the plants from bolting to flower too quickly in long, hot days. Harvest by pinching young leaves and shoot tips starting around a month after sowing, which also delays flowering and keeps the plant producing tender new growth for weeks. It tolerates heat and some drought better than spinach or lettuce, making it a dependable summer green when cool-season leafy crops have failed. Cook briefly by steaming or sautéing, similar to amaranth greens, to preserve texture and nutrients.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

common_name: Royal Cape Plumbago (Compact Deep-Blue Cape Plumbago)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Royal Cape's deeper blue flowers and denser habit make it a strong choice for foundation beds or large containers where the sprawling straight species would be too loose.

directions: Royal Cape is a selection of Cape plumbago bred for noticeably deeper, more saturated blue flowers than the pale sky-blue of the straight species, held on a somewhat denser, more compact shrub. It flowers nearly continuously from spring through frost in zone 9, drawing Cassius blue butterflies, which use plumbago as a larval host plant, along with other pollinators. Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; it is fast-growing, drought-tolerant once established, and tolerant of the poor sandy soils and salt spray common along the Gulf Coast. In zone 9 winters, hard freezes often kill the top growth, but the plant resprouts readily from the roots and returns to bloom by late spring; cut back damaged stems in late winter to clean up the plant before new growth begins.

common_name: Sparky Tecoma (Tricolor Orange-Red-Yellow Hybrid Yellow Bells)

planting.note: Set out container plants after the last frost in full sun in well-drained, lean, xeric-tolerant soil; Sparky was bred for a compact habit and multicolor flowers compared to solid-yellow standard esperanza.

directions: Sparky is a hybrid tecoma bred for trumpet-shaped flowers that open orange-red in the throat and shade out to golden yellow at the petal edges, a warm tricolor effect that stands out from the solid yellow of straight-species esperanza. It blooms heavily from early summer through the first hard frost and draws hummingbirds reliably throughout that window. Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean soil; it is markedly drought-tolerant once established and thrives in the heat of a Gulf South or desert Southwest summer. In zone 9, expect the top growth to die back in a hard freeze; cut the dead stems to the ground in late winter and the plant resprouts vigorously from the base and blooms the same season.
sources: Arizona Municipal Water Users Association — low-water landscape plant database
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tecoma in Southern Gardens

common_name: Bells of Fire Tecoma (Deep Orange-Red Hybrid Yellow Bells)

planting.note: Set out container plants after the last frost in full sun in well-drained, lean, xeric-tolerant soil; a compact hybrid tecoma bred for saturated orange-red flower color rather than the yellow of standard esperanza.

directions: Bells of Fire is a hybrid tecoma selected for trumpet-shaped flowers in a deep, saturated orange-red that reads much hotter in the landscape than the golden yellow of straight-species esperanza, blooming heavily from early summer into fall and drawing hummingbirds throughout. Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean soil; like other tecoma hybrids it is highly heat- and drought-tolerant once established, making it a strong choice for xeric borders and low-water landscapes. In zone 9, a hard freeze typically kills the top growth back to the ground; remove the dead stems in late winter and the plant resprouts vigorously from the base, usually flowering again by midsummer.
sources: Arizona Municipal Water Users Association — low-water landscape plant database
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tecoma in Southern Gardens
